name: ACCRINT

args.name: issue
args.about: the day the bond was issued

args.name: first_interest
args.about: the day of its first interest payment

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: rate
args.about: the yearly interest rate it pays, like 0.05 for 5%

args.name: par
args.about: its face value (1000 if left out)

args.name: frequency
args.about: interest payments a year: 1, 2 or 4

args.name: basis

args.name: calc_method
args.about: TRUE to count from the issue date (the usual), FALSE from the last payment

about: The interest a bond has earned since it was issued but not yet paid out, which a buyer pays the seller.

example.why: A 1000 bond paying 5% a year earns 50 a year; three months is a quarter of that, 12.50.

name: ACCRINTM

args.name: issue
args.about: the day the security was issued

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day it pays out (its maturity)

args.name: rate
args.about: the yearly interest rate, like 0.04 for 4%

args.name: par
args.about: its face value (1000 if left out)

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The interest earned by a security that pays all its interest in one go at the end.

example.why: 4% of 5000 is 200 a year; nine months earn three quarters of that, 150.

name: DISC

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity

args.name: pr

args.name: basis

about: The yearly discount rate of a security bought below what it pays out, like a Treasury bill.

example.why: You pay 96 and get 100 a year later: the discount of 4 is 4% of 100.

name: FVSCHEDULE

args.name: principal
args.about: the amount you start with

args.name: schedule
args.about: the interest rates, one for each year (or period)

about: What an amount grows to when each year earns a different interest rate.

example.why: 1000 × 1.02 × 1.03 × 1.04 = 1092.62: each year's interest is added before the next year's is worked out.

name: INTRATE

args.name: settlement

args.name: investment

args.name: redemption
args.about: the amount you get back

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The yearly interest rate of an investment that pays everything back on one day.

example.why: 200 extra on 10000 is 2% in half a year, so 4% a year.

name: PRICEDISC

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity

args.name: discount
args.about: the yearly discount rate, like 0.04 for 4%

args.name: redemption
args.about: what it pays out per 100 of face value

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The price per 100 of a security sold at a discount, like a Treasury bill.

example.why: A 4% yearly discount for half a year takes 2 off the 100 it pays out.

name: PRICEMAT

args.name: settlement

args.name: maturity

args.name: issue

args.name: rate

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The price per 100 of a security that pays all its interest at the end.

example.why: It pays 105 at the end; to earn 6% a year you'd pay 100.48 for it, less the 1.25 of interest it had already earned, 99.23.

name: RECEIVED

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity

args.about: the amount you pay

args.name: discount
args.about: the yearly discount rate, like 0.04 for 4%

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: How much a security bought at a discount pays out at the end.

example.why: Half a year at a 4% discount takes 2% off: 9800 is 98% of 10000.

name: YIELDDISC

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity

args.about: what it pays out per 100 of face value

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The yearly return of a security bought below what it pays out.

example.why: You gain 2 on the 98 you paid in half a year: 2.04%, so 4.08% a year.

notes: DISC gives the discount on what it pays out; this gives the return on what you paid.

name: YIELDMAT

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity

args.name: issue
args.about: the day it was issued

args.name: rate

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: The yearly return of a security that pays all its interest at the end.

example.why: Paying 99 for something that pays 105 at the end, less the interest already earned, gives about 6.3% a year, a bit above the 5% it pays.

name: CUMIPMT

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per payment, like 0.06/12 for 6% a year paid monthly

args.name: nper

args.name: pv

about: How much interest you pay on a loan between two payments.

example.why: In the first year of a five-year car loan of 20000 at 6%, 1103.81 of the payments is interest. It shows as a minus because it's money paid out.

name: CUMPRINC

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per payment, like 0.06/12 for 6% a year paid monthly

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments in all

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

args.name: start_period
args.about: the first payment to count

args.name: end_period
args.about: the last payment to count

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: How much of a loan you pay off (leaving out interest) between two payments.

example.why: In the first year of a five-year car loan of 20000 at 6%, 3536.06 of what's borrowed is paid back; the rest of the payments is interest.

name: DB

args.name: cost
args.about: what the thing cost

args.name: salvage
args.about: what it's worth at the end of its life

args.name: life
args.about: how many years it lasts

args.name: period
args.about: which year to work out

args.name: month
args.about: months in the first year (12 if left out)

about: How much value something loses in a year, losing the same share of what's left each year (fixed-declining balance).

example.why: Losing 36.9% a year takes 10000 down to 1000 in five years; the first year loses 3690. The cell is given a money format.

name: DDB

args.name: cost
args.about: what the thing cost

args.name: salvage
args.about: what it's worth at the end of its life

args.name: life
args.about: how many years it lasts

args.name: period
args.about: which year to work out

args.name: factor
args.about: how fast it loses value (2 if left out, twice the straight-line rate)

about: How much value something loses in a year, losing more in the early years (double-declining balance).

example.why: Each year loses 2/5 of what's left: 4000 the first year, then 40% of the 6000 left is 2400. The cell is given a money format.

name: DOLLARDE

args.name: fractional_dollar
args.about: a price written with a fraction after the point, like 1.02 for 1 and 2/16

args.name: fraction
args.about: the bottom of the fraction, like 16

about: Turns a price written as whole units and a fraction into an ordinary decimal.

example.why: Bond prices are sometimes quoted in sixteenths: 101.08 means 101 and 8/16, which is 101.5.

name: DOLLARFR

args.name: decimal_dollar
args.about: an ordinary decimal price

args.name: fraction
args.about: the bottom of the fraction, like 16

about: Turns a decimal price into whole units and a fraction, as some bond prices are quoted.

example.why: 0.5 is 8/16, so 101.5 is written 101.08: 101 and 8 sixteenths.

name: EFFECT

args.name: nominal_rate
args.about: the yearly rate as advertised, like 0.06 for 6%

args.name: npery
args.about: how many times a year interest is added, like 12

about: The rate you really earn or pay in a year when interest is added several times a year.

example.why: 6% a year added monthly is 0.5% a month; with interest on interest that makes about 6.17% over the year.

name: FV

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period, like 0.04/12 for 4% a year paid monthly

args.name: nper
args.about: how many periods

args.name: pmt
args.about: the amount paid in each period (negative for money you put in)

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount at the start (negative for money you put in; 0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: What savings grow to after regular payments and interest.

example.why: Putting 200 a month into savings at 4% for ten years (24000 in all) grows to about 29450 with the interest.

name: IPMT

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period, like 0.05/12 for 5% a year paid monthly

args.name: per
args.about: which payment to look at, from 1

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments in all

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

args.name: fv
args.about: what's left at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: How much of one loan payment is interest.

example.why: In the first month of a 25-year mortgage of 200000 at 5%, the interest is 200000 × 5% ÷ 12 = 833.33.

notes: PPMT gives the rest of the payment, the part that pays off the loan.

name: IRR

args.name: values
args.about: the money in and out, one per year, starting with what you put in as a minus

args.name: guess
args.about: a rate to start searching from (0.1 if left out)

about: The yearly return of an investment from the money paid in and out of it each year.

example.why: Putting in 10000 and getting back 3000, 4000 and 5000 over three years is like earning about 8.9% a year.

notes: XIRR works with payments on any dates.

name: ISPMT

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period

args.name: per
args.about: which period, counting from 0

args.name: nper
args.about: how many periods in all

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

about: The interest in one period of a loan that pays back the same amount of the loan each period.

example.why: Paying back 2000 a year, after the first year 6000 is still owed: 5% of 6000 is 300 of interest.

name: MIRR

args.name: values
args.about: the money in and out, one per period, starting with what you put in as a minus

args.name: finance_rate
args.about: the interest you pay on money you borrow

args.name: reinvest_rate
args.about: the interest you earn on money you get back

about: The yearly return of an investment when the money you get back is saved at a different rate.

example.why: If what comes back each year only earns 3% in the bank, the 10000 grows less than IRR assumes: about 7.15% a year instead of 8.9%.

name: NOMINAL

args.name: effect_rate
args.about: the rate really earned in a year, like 0.0617

args.name: npery
args.about: how many times a year interest is added, like 12

about: The advertised yearly rate that gives a real yearly rate when interest is added several times a year.

example.why: To really earn 5% a year with interest added every quarter, the advertised rate need only be about 4.91%.

name: NPER

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period

args.name: pmt
args.about: the amount paid each period (negative for money you pay)

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed, or what you start with

args.name: fv
args.about: what's left at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: How many payments it takes to pay off a loan or reach a savings goal.

example.why: Paying 150 a month off a 3000 credit card at 18% a year takes about 24 months.

name: NPV

args.name: rate
args.about: the yearly rate to discount by, like what the money would earn elsewhere

args.name: value1
args.about: the money in (or out, as a minus) at the end of year 1

args.name: value2
args.about: more years' money

about: What future money in and out is worth today, given what money could earn meanwhile.

example.why: At 5% a year, 3000 next year is worth 3000 ÷ 1.05 today, 4000 in two years 4000 ÷ 1.05², and so on; the three add up to 10804.45.

notes: The first value is a year away. Money you pay today goes outside: =NPV(rate,…)+today's amount.

name: PDURATION

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount you start with

args.name: fv
args.about: the amount you want to reach

about: How many periods it takes for money to grow to an amount at a given rate.

example.why: At 4% a year, money doubles in about 17.7 years.

name: PMT

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period, like 0.05/12 for 5% a year paid monthly

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

args.name: fv
args.about: what's left at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: The regular payment that pays off a loan, with interest, over a number of periods.

example.why: A 25-year mortgage of 200000 at 5% costs about 1169 a month; it's a minus because it's money you pay.

name: PPMT

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period, like 0.05/12 for 5% a year paid monthly

args.name: per
args.about: which payment to look at, from 1

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments in all

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

args.name: fv
args.about: what's left at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: How much of one loan payment pays off the loan itself, leaving out the interest.

example.why: The first monthly payment of a 25-year mortgage of 200000 at 5% is about 1169, of which 833.33 is interest, so only about 336 pays off the loan.

name: PV

args.name: rate
args.about: the interest rate per period

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments

args.name: pmt
args.about: the amount paid each period (negative for money you pay)

args.name: fv
args.about: a lump sum at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

about: What a series of future payments is worth today, like how much you can borrow for a monthly payment.

example.why: If you can pay 300 a month for four years at 6%, you can borrow about 12774.

name: RATE

args.name: nper
args.about: how many payments

args.name: pmt
args.about: the amount paid each period (negative for money you pay)

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount borrowed

args.name: fv
args.about: what's left at the end (0 if left out)

args.name: type
args.about: 0 for payments at the end of each period (the usual), 1 at the start

args.name: guess
args.about: a rate to start searching from (0.1 if left out)

about: The interest rate per period of a loan or savings plan.

example.why: Borrowing 12000 and paying 300 a month for four years (14400 in all) is a rate of about 0.77% a month, 9.24% a year.

name: RRI

args.name: nper
args.about: how many periods

args.name: pv
args.about: the amount at the start

args.name: fv
args.about: the amount at the end

about: The steady yearly growth rate that takes one amount to another.

example.why: Growing from 10000 to 14000 in five years is like about 7% a year, with growth on growth.

name: SLN

args.name: cost
args.about: what the thing cost

args.name: salvage
args.about: what it's worth at the end of its life

args.name: life
args.about: how many years it lasts

about: How much value something loses each year when it loses the same amount every year (straight-line).

example.why: It loses 9000 over five years, 1800 a year. The cell is given a money format.

name: SYD

args.name: cost
args.about: what the thing cost

args.name: salvage
args.about: what it's worth at the end of its life

args.name: life
args.about: how many years it lasts

args.name: per
args.about: which year to work out

about: How much value something loses in a year, losing a bit less each year (sum-of-years' digits).

example.why: The years count 5+4+3+2+1 = 15 shares; the first year loses 5/15 of the 9000, 3000. The cell is given a money format.

name: TBILLEQ

args.name: settlement
args.about: the day you buy it

args.name: maturity
args.about: the day it pays out, within a year

args.name: discount
args.about: the yearly discount rate, like 0.04 for 4%

about: The bond-style yearly return of a Treasury bill, to compare it with bonds.

example.why: A 4% discount for 181 days means paying about 98 for 100, a return of a little over 4% a year.

name: TBILLPRICE

args.name: settlement

args.name: maturity

args.name: discount
args.about: the yearly discount rate, like 0.04 for 4%

about: The price per 100 of a Treasury bill.

name: XIRR

args.name: values

args.name: guess
args.about: a rate to start searching from (0.1 if left out)

about: The yearly return of an investment whose payments come on any dates.

example.why: 10000 put in and 12000 back over two years, some of it early, is like earning about 13.3% a year.

notes: IRR is the same for payments a year apart.

name: XNPV

args.name: rate

args.name: values
args.about: the money in and out

args.name: dates
args.about: the date of each amount; the first is today

about: What money in and out on any dates is worth on the first date.

example.why: At 5% a year the later amounts are worth 11166.90 on 1 January 2026, so after the 10000 paid the investment is 1166.90 ahead.

example.why: A five-year bond pays interest along the way, so on average its money comes back in about 4.4 years.

name: MDURATION

example.why: Paying 95 for a bond paying 5% that gives back 100 in five years earns about 6.18% a year.

about: How much value something loses in a year under the French accounts rules, losing more early on.

example.why: A 15% rate means a life of about 6.7 years, so it's multiplied by 2.5 to 37.5%: the first year loses 3750, and the second 37.5% of the 6250 left, 2344 in whole units.

notes: As in other spreadsheet apps, it gives #NUM! when 1/rate (the life in years) is 3 or less or between 4 and 5, so a 20% or 25% rate doesn't work. AMORLINC loses the same amount every year.
